1785754639398474229 [2024-05-01] @relic_radiation 💜 54 🔁 5
really interesting point by Kush in this video:

> Western medicine is definitionally the study of interventions that work for large groups of people

> Ayurveda's approach is "how can we train specific practitioners to best help the specific people in front of them, repeatedly" https://t.co/NIi7eFMQ4H
  [Quoting Tweet 1777822710267322686 (missing)]
↓
1785755369022931350 [2024-05-01] @relic_radiation 💜 9
this is a whole different frame! and I'm not convinced 'the underlying structure of human health' is a good fit for large-group-study approach. 

'large-group-study' is more an answer to "yo what if we applied stats to health" and not "what's the best approach to health"
↓
1785755788360999325 [2024-05-01] @relic_radiation 💜 8 [(SEED) type=quote_of_root]
though actually... I think you could still do stats x health. but I'd start by putting the locus on "practitioners and their outcomes" rather than "interventions"

bc practitioners can account for personal mazes, interventions kinda can't https://t.co/j77JM7Uq6J
  [Quoting @eshear: Parenting and education studies be like, “to get children out of their personal mazes we tried the always-turn-left, always-turn-right, and zig-zag-alternating interventions. Zig-zag performed the worst, and we saw only mild lift from always-turn-right and always-turn-left.”]

1785757480330691061 [2024-05-01] @relic_radiation 💜 11
when studying interventions, there's a failure mode where "consensus on what's the best intervention" can accidentally converge to "the intervention that is easiest to study" which is NOT necessarily the best intervention.

for example, CBT definitely isn't the best therapy
